🪔 Hello, Sunday, and happy Diwali. Smart Brevity™ count: 1,986 words ... 7½ mins. Erica Pandey is your weekend host. Edited by Andrew Pantazi.

🥊 Situational awareness: UFC CEO Dana White says he'll meet with President Trump tomorrow about Trump's offer to make him the new White House press secretary. Go deeper.

  • 🏛️ Democratic House members and members-elect are being bombarded with phone calls and emails urging them not to elect Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker, more than a dozen lawmakers and aides tell Axios' Andrew Solender. Actor Mark Ruffalo's post on X calling for "a new speaker" has been driving much of the outreach. Keep reading.
  • 🔎 Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.), incoming chair of Senate Foreign Relations, said he'll investigate spying allegations about a Chinese businesswoman who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
 
 
1 big thing: Texas, Texas, Texas
 

Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios
 

No state looms larger, more dominant or more instructive about the future of American politics, governance and AI than Texas, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen write in a "Behind the Curtain" column.

  • Why it matters: Texas is suddenly — and unexpectedly — the American story. It's the battleground and proving ground for immigration policy, AI, data center growth, Hispanic voting patterns, and the direction of the Democratic Party.

Put simply, it seems nearly impossible for Republicans to retain the presidency in 2028 without the Lone Star State. And it seems nearly impossible for AI to keep growing so fast if Texas rejects or dramatically slows it.

  • Texas is so populous, so wealthy, so Hispanic, so energy-rich — and now so top-to-bottom blue — that both parties see it as a de facto nation-state capable of reordering … everything.

👀 "Texas is everything," Steve Bannon, one of the top voices of MAGA, told us. Bannon has been so Texas-obsessed all year that he took his influential podcast, "War Room," on the road to the "forward lines" of Texas for months at a time.

  • Bannon said Texas needs to be an early focus for Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff. Houston Mayor John Whitmire on Friday directed police to limit cooperation with ICE, saying: "Elections matter." Bannon said he expects many more such actions, with Texas becoming a sanctuary state "quickly unless dramatic action is taken."
  • "Trump is going to be forced to federalize the border," Bannon said, either with National Guard troops or federal law-enforcement agents.

The big picture: Texas was red as blood on Nov. 2, the day before midterms. Now it'll have a Democratic governor ... lieutenant governor ... attorney general ... comptroller ... land commissioner ... agriculture commissioner ... Texas House ... and U.S. senator, 37-year-old James Talarico.

  • Talarico won by double digits over state Attorney General Ken Paxton, and Gina Hinojosa — who'll be Texas' first Latina governor — upset three-term Gov. Greg Abbott. Democrats won all four state Supreme Court seats on the ballot and are set to flip Texas' Board of Education.
  • The new Texas House speaker is likely to be an 87-year-old Black woman, Senfronia Thompson, a Houston Democrat first elected during the Watergate era.

Everything's bigger in Texas, especially in politics going forward:

1. ⚡ South Texas' border counties broke the GOP's thesis. Republicans built their Texas future on South Texas Hispanics, based on President Trump's performance there in 2024.

  • Talarico won Hidalgo by 46 points, Cameron by 38 and Webb by 47. Trump had narrowly carried all three!
  • The lesson: The Valley didn't realign. It swung — or came home to Democrats, as many South Texans would say.

2. 🧳 Immigration came home, too. Republicans' border-security argument was undermined as President Trump's ICE, cheered on by Abbott, hit South Texas' rural counties and then moved hard-line enforcement into cities across the state.

  • Hidalgo voters were driven by a sluggish economy and the historic immigration crackdown. In Harris County (Houston), voters cited immigration, corruption and GOP leaders' policies as motivating their votes.

3. 🦾 Texas is now ground zero for the AI wars. Elon Musk, the world's richest person, moved to business-friendly Texas from California along with other tech elites, and brought along Tesla's headquarters.

  • Musk posted a reminder yesterday to incoming leaders: "SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government. ... As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas."
  • Musk made himself a midterm issue, spending $225 million on races in Texas — about half of his national total. Talarico ran straight at him: "This Senate seat doesn't belong to Elon Musk." After the rout, Musk said on X that data centers in space were looking "pretty appealing."

🔌 Texas was on track to become home to one of the world's largest concentrations of data centers, but that buildout is now at risk. In August, 57% of Texan registered voters in a University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll opposed a data center in their own community, including 43% of Republicans, 60% of suburbanites and 60% of rural voters.

  • Gov. Greg Abbott (R) tried to pivot from his bullishness on data centers but still lost reelection. On Aug. 3, he paused new data center grid connections.

4. 🫏 All-of-the-above energy now has a Democratic landlord. Texas pumps the oil, drills the gas, harnesses the wind, runs its own grid — and powers the AI boom.

  • Hinojosa pledged a moratorium on new data center approvals until the Legislature passes protections in 2027. One energy lawyer called it "a brand-new day in Texas" for policy once considered settled.
  • The challenge: Wage war on oil and gas, and Texas snaps back red. Govern like Texans have through much of the state's history, and Democrats could get a lease measured in decades.

5. 🗳️ The Hispanic vote is America's biggest swing bloc. Texas had a record-setting surge in Latino turnout, and Talarico won 68% of them.

  • Two years ago, that same bloc gave Trump the Valley. This time, the more heavily Hispanic the county, the heavier the leftward shift.

6. 🧮 Republicans suddenly have a 2028 math problem. Texas has the second-most electoral votes, after California. Take out the Lone Star State's 40 electoral votes and Trump would have had only a two-vote cushion in 2024.

The bottom line: For 50 years, California told you where America was headed. Now Texas does — and it just changed its mind.

2. 💥 Scoop: First major Miller shakeup
 
Stephen Miller in the presidential limousine after arriving in West Palm Beach on Friday night. Photo: Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images

White House deputy chief of staff Richard Walters is leaving the administration, the first major departure in an expected staff shakeup as incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller takes charge, Axios' Alex Isenstadt reports.

  • Why it matters: The exit of one of outgoing chief of staff Susie Wiles' allies signals a changing of the guard inside the West Wing, with Miller's team poised to move into more powerful roles.

Walters was one of Wiles' closest political lieutenants, with a relationship stretching back more than a decade. He's a veteran Republican operative who served as the longest-tenured chief of staff in RNC history.

  • Walters resigned Friday, the same day that Trump announced Miller would replace Wiles.

Read on.
 
 
3. 🏛️ House poised to impeach Hegseth
 
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks at the Pentagon in a video last week. Image: X via Reuters

House Republican leaders are bracing for enough GOP defections to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the measure comes to a vote this week, Axios' Kate Santaliz reports.

  • Why it matters: Republicans defeated in Tuesday's election-night bloodbath have little left to lose and could be more willing to impeach Hegseth, whose support has eroded since the start of the Iran war.

Hegseth doesn't have "a lot of love" on Capitol Hill, retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Fox News. Bacon told Axios he's undecided on this week's vote.

  • Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) plans to force a vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth for allegedly defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran.

The other side: Hegseth fought back with a video on X on Thursday, castigating "sham articles of impeachment" as "political theater."

  • Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to Axios: "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. ... Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office."

Reality check: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate — a threshold that would be difficult to achieve even after Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

4. 📊 Data du jour: Massive turnout
 

Data: University of Florida Election Lab. Chart: Bruce Mehlman

President Trump energizes Americans like no other national candidate in history:

  • Bruce Mehlman points out in a special post-election edition of his popular "Six-Chart Sunday" on Substack that preliminary estimates of Tuesday's turnout was the second highest for a midterm in more than a century — topped only by 2018, during Trump's first term.

"Love him or loathe him, Trump energizes midterm voters like nothing else — more than Vietnam, more than Watergate, more than civil rights," Mehlman told me.

  • The largest share of eligible voters turned out in Maine (65.7%), Minnesota (65.2%) and Michigan (63.2%). All three states fueled the blue wave.

🔭 Zoom out: The past two presidential elections drew the most total votes (partly a function of population) of any in history.

  • 2020: 158.4 million votes, when Joe Biden unseated Donald Trump.
  • 2024: 155.2 million votes, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris.

5. 🇮🇱 Bibi rival tapped to form Israeli government
 
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, in Tel Aviv on election night, Oct. 28. Photo: Shir Torem/Reuters

Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced yesterday that he'll task Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, with forming a new government, dealing a major setback to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

  • Eisenkot will have 28 days to form a new government.

Why it matters: This is the closest Netanyahu has come to losing power since 2021. But deep divisions could still prevent rivals from forming a government, Axios' Barak Ravid writes.

6. 🫨 Charted: Dems' youthquake
 
Data: Preliminary results from Times Voter Trends. Chart: Arfa Momin/The New York Times

Younger voters — sick of the status quo and looking for leaders closer to their own age — powered the midterm rout of the GOP.

  • Why it matters: Trump's 2024 success with Gen Z voters, especially young men, fueled talk of a generational shift toward Republicans. Tuesday's results tell a different story, Axios' Russell Contreras writes.

Young men swung by a stunning 39 points toward Democrats compared with '24, according to The New York Times' Voter Trends. In Texas, they swung by 50 points.

  • Young women, already reliably blue voters, shifted 27 points to the left.

7. 🗳️ Ossoff wins Crooked Con straw poll
 

Ben Rhodes (left) and Tommy Vietor hold a live taping of "Pod Save the World" at yesterday's Crooked Con in Washington. Photo: Mike Allen/Axios
 

Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia was the runaway winner of yesterday's Crooked Con straw poll for the 2028 Democratic nominee, taken by Crooked Media, parent of "Pod Save America," at D.C.'s convention center.

  • Ossoff won 38.4% of the 990 responses, followed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York (16.6%) and Pete Buttigieg (13.9%). The rest were in single digits.
  • The straw poll asked attendees who they'd most want to face as the Republican nominee. Vice President Vance drew nearly half the vote.

I'm told Crooked Con had 3,500 registered attendees, up from last year's 2,500.

8. 🐊 1 for the road: Holiday hot spots
 
Data: Kayak. Table: Sami Sparber/Axios

Florida is home to five of this year's top 10 trending domestic holiday destinations, Axios' Sami Sparber writes from Kayak search data.

  • Why it matters: As airfares climb, travelers are "chasing sunshine without blowing the holiday budget," Kayak's Kayla DeLoache tells Axios.

The big picture: Booking company Hopper reports travel this holiday season is on track to be the most expensive in at least a decade, largely because of soaring jet fuel costs.

  • Domestic fares on Kayak averaged $417 for Thanksgiving and $418 for Christmas and New Year's — compared with last year's $317 and $351, respectively.
